components.title: Extract functional requirements from description
components.teaches: Using a worked example, students parse an unstructured product description to list functional requirements, grouping them by user goal. They apply a template to capture preconditions, postconditions, and triggers.

components.title: Write use case main success scenario
components.teaches: Students construct the main success scenario for a use case, writing numbered steps that show actor–system interactions. They ensure each step is atomic, observable, and follows the spec guidelines.

components.title: Write use case extensions and alternate flows
components.teaches: Students extend the main scenario with extension points, alternate flows, and exception handling, using the same numbering scheme. They learn to reference extension conditions and maintain traceability.

components.title: Create system boundary context diagram
components.teaches: In a live demo, the instructor builds a UML context diagram showing the system, actors, and external systems. Students see how the diagram validates the actor list and boundary decisions.

components.title: Prioritize use cases with MoSCoW
components.teaches: Students compare MoSCoW, business value, and risk‑based prioritization techniques on a sample use case set. They decide which use cases belong to Must, Should, Could, Won't for the first release.

components.title: Validate use cases against spec guidelines
components.teaches: Through guided discussion, students apply a checklist derived from spec‑driven guidelines to assess completeness, consistency, and testability of their use cases. They identify missing preconditions and ambiguous steps.

components.title: Map use cases to spec-driven framework artifacts
components.teaches: Students learn how each use case maps to downstream artifacts such as feature files, acceptance criteria, and test cases in a spec‑driven development framework. They trace a use case through the pipeline.

components.title: Case study: product description to use case model
components.teaches: A full case study walks through transforming a realistic product description into a complete use case model, including actors, boundary, scenarios, and prioritization. Students analyse each transformation decision.

components.title: Common pitfalls and quality checklist
components.teaches: Discussion of frequent errors such as actor overload, vague steps, and missing extensions. Students use a quality checklist to review a peer's use case specification and suggest improvements.

components.title: Summary and transition to spec-driven frameworks
components.teaches: Recap of the use case engineering process, emphasizing how the produced artifacts feed into spec‑driven development frameworks. Students outline next steps for automated test generation.

video.description:
Learn how to make Use Case Diagrams in this tutorial. Both beginners and intermediate UML diagrammers will find all the necessary training and examples on systems, actors, use cases, and include and extend relationships.

UML Use Case Diagrams show a system or application; then they show the people, organizations, or other systems that interact with it; and finally, they show a basic flow of what the system or application does.

This tutorial explains the four main characteristics of Use Case Diagrams: systems, actors, use cases, and relationships.

A system is whatever you’re developing. It could be a website, a software component, a business process, an app, or any number of other things.

video.description:
What is Spec-Driven Development and how does it improve AI coding for larger projects?
Spec-Driven Development is an emerging AI coding workflow where AI agents generate code based on structured specifications instead of simple prompts. As AI tools like GitHub Copilot and ChatGPT become common in software development, developers need better ways to manage large AI-generated codebases.
